description: Somos un equipo enfocado en innovación educativa, tecnología e ingeniería. Nuestro reto será desarrollar una experiencia interactiva para entrenar a futuros astronautas mediante la toma de decisiones reales sobre energía, alimentos, radiación y supervivencia en la Luna o Marte. Buscamos personas interesadas en programación, diseño, IA, educación STEM, gamificación y comunicación. Valoramos la creatividad, el trabajo en equipo y las ideas que puedan generar impacto educativo real.
summary: It's a 2.5D educational simulator for children aged 7 to 12, inspired by NASA is upcoming Artemis missions. Players manage a lunar base at the South Pole with the goal of surviving until Day 180, learning to make real-world decisions about energy, oxygen, water, food, radiation, and space exploration. Instead of traditional quizzes, learning happens through an interactive simulation where every decision has visible consequences. Students allocate power among critical systems, manage limited resources, respond to emergencies, explore the lunar surface with a rover, grow food inspired by space research, and collaborate with Cosmo, a virtual mentor that encourages critical thinking. The project uses data and knowledge from NASA DONKI, OSDR, and Artemis to connect real science with gameplay. It runs in a browser, with no installation or accounts required, even without an internet connection. Our goal is to inspire the next generation of explorers, scientists, and engineers, demonstrating that any child can learn to think like a mission commander and be part of humanity's future journey from the Moon to Mars.
details:
What exactly does it do?

MoonHopKids Academy is an interactive 2.5D simulator for managing a space station at the Lunar South Pole and training for a mission to Mars, designed specifically for children and schoolchildren aged 7 to 12. Instead of presenting space science as a multiple-choice school exam or passive reading, it puts the student in charge of Artemis Base with a clear goal: to learn how to manage interconnected systems to survive until the arrival of the relief crew on Day 180 .

At the start, the student chooses their age range using visual cards ( 7 to 9 years old - Cadet Mode , focused on visual minigames, simple whole numbers and step-by-step guidance; or 10 to 12 years old - Explorer Mode , with engineering challenges, reading scientific graphs and greater operational demands) and customizes their astronaut's suit and visor.

How does it work? The heart of the project translates NASA's life support physics and engineering into a live simulation where no decision is arbitrary and every resource is interconnected .

  1. Physical Coupling and Live Causal Diagram: From the Power Console, the child distributes electrical power (in easily calculated whole numbers) among four subsystems: Life Support (ECLSS), Thermal Control, Greenhouse/ISRU, and Science/Communications. An animated piping diagram shows in real time how saving battery power by reducing life support decreases oxygen production by electrolysis, reduces water recycling, and accumulates CO2 in the cabin. Before confirming any decision, the resource panel bars flash, showing what will increase and what will decrease.
  2. Real-Time Space Weather (NASA DONKI) and the 12 South Pole Sectors: The game connects to the NASA DONKI API to read recent solar activity (or use curated historical storms if the school doesn't have internet access). It models the real-world difference between a Solar Flare (SFL) that instantly cuts out radio, Solar Energetic Particles (SEP) that force moonwalks to be aborted within minutes, and a Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) that provides 1 to 3 days' warning to fortify the shelter with water bags and regolith.
  3. EVA Exploration, LTV Rover, and Space Biology (OSDR): The player exits through the airlocks onto a map divided into 12 real-world sectors of the Lunar South Pole (Shackleton, Cabeus, Malapert, Haworth, Leibnitz). They drive the LTV Rover, turning on its headlights in perpetually shadowed craters to collect water ice, coordinate with their two crewmates via radio, analyze samples with a magnifying glass in the laboratory, and plant three real-world crops studied in NASA OSDR ( Outredgeous Lettuce, Apogee Wheat, and Arabidopsis in regolith ).
  4. Cosmo (Socratic Mentor) and Second Chance Protocol: Our companion robot, Cosmo , accompanies the child as a spatial conscience. Before an emergency, he poses a brief question to encourage reflection; if a resource reaches zero for the first time, he activates a rescue protocol with real costs instead of frustrating the child with a Game Over ; and in each mission, he unlocks a "NASA Secret" with verifiable real data.

What are the benefits and what do we hope to achieve?

  • Zero barriers for public and rural schools: We developed the entire simulator in a single self-contained HTML file (~280 KB) that runs at 60 FPS on any computer, tablet or mobile browser without installing anything, without asking for accounts or personal data, and working 100% offline if there is no connection in the classroom.
  • Teacher-ready assessment: Includes a STEM Report generator aligned with NGSS standards and a downloadable Official Artemis Passport in PNG image with the decision-making badges earned by the student.
  • Our goal from San Vicente de Cañete is to demonstrate that any child aged 7 to 12 can learn to think like a NASA engineer and mission commander, awakening STEM vocations for the generation that will take humanity from the Moon to Mars.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software do we use?

  • Native Languages ​​and APIs (Zero-Dependency): Developed entirely with pure HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript (ES6+) , without heavy engines or external libraries that require downloading.
  • 2.5D Graphics Engine and UI: HTML5 Canvas 2D API (with frustum culling optimization , terrain caching in 9 offscreen chunks , dynamic lighting by composition masks and vector avatars in dynamic SVG ).
  • Procedural Audio and Voice Engine: Native Web Audio API (ambient synthesizer in D minor pentatonic scale, filtered noise generator for steps in regolith, locks, rover and Geiger dosimeter, plus a dynamic compressor on the master bus) and Web Speech API (speechSynthesis) with automatic audio ducking for reading accessible to young children.
  • Data Connection and Persistence: asynchronous fetching to api.nasa.gov/DONKI and osdr.nasa.gov with deterministic local backup and manual saving to localStorage.
